items.markdown:
![Inflation: What It Is and How to Control Inflation Rates](https://api.dataforseo.com/cdn/i/05291010-1824-0066-0000-87f1586ac01c:4)
Inflation is `the general and sustained increase in the price level of goods and services within an economy over a period of time` . When this happens, each unit of your currency buys a smaller percentage of a good or service, meaning the purchasing power of money decreases.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflation)[[2]](https://www.tutor2u.net/economics/topics/inflation)[[3]](https://www.britannica.com/money/inflation-economics)

Key Concepts

- **Purchasing Power:** As average prices go up, a single unit of currency buys fewer items. If inflation is 3%, a basket of goods that cost £100 last year now costs £103.[[1]](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/guides/zrwtmfr/revision/5)[[2]](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/monetary-policy/inflation)
- **Inflation Rate:** This is the annualized percentage change in a general price index (e.g., the Consumer Price Index, or CPI). It indicates how quickly prices are rising.[[1]](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/explainers/what-is-inflation)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflation)
- **Deflation:** The exact opposite of inflation; a sustained decrease in the general price level of goods and services.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflation)
- **Disinflation:** A situation where the *rate* of inflation is slowing down. Even if the inflation rate drops, overall prices may still be increasing, just at a slower pace than before.[[1]](https://www.ons.gov.uk/aboutus/usingpublicdatatoproducestatistics/learningaboutdata/learnmoreaboutwhoweareandwhatwedo/whatisinflationandhowdowecalculateit)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflation)

What Causes Inflation?

- **Demand-Pull:** Occurs when the overall demand for goods and services outpaces the economy's ability to produce them, driving up prices.
- **Cost-Push:** Happens when the cost of producing goods and services increases (e.g., higher wages, more expensive raw materials), and businesses raise their prices to maintain their profit margins.
- **Money Supply Growth:** When there is an increase in the volume of money and credit in an economy, money can lose its relative value.[[1]](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/inflation)[[2]](https://www.blackrock.com/us/individual/education/inflation)[[3]](https://www.xero.com/uk/glossary/inflation/)[[4]](https://www.britannica.com/money/inflation-economics)[[5]](https://www.mckinsey.com/featured-insights/mckinsey-explainers/what-is-inflation)

How is it Measured?Governments use baskets of typical household goods and services to track these price shifts over time. You can view current inflation data, economic metrics, and tracking tools through major national statistics agencies like the Office for National Statistics in the UK, the Bureau of Labor Statistics in the US, or central banks like the [Bank of England](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/monetary-policy/inflation).[[1]](https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/ld201719/ldselect/ldeconaf/246/24604.htm)[[2]](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/explainers)[[3]](https://www.rba.gov.au/education/resources/explainers/inflation-and-its-measurement.html)
